title_jp: {田中家|たなかけ}の{晩|ばん|evening}ご{飯|はん}
context: This afternoon Tanaka-san picked you up at Guesthouse Kaze and drove you to the farm. Now it's your first dinner with him and his wife Keiko. Today: asking for things politely at someone's table, and being looked after.

phrases.jp: お{醤油|しょうゆ|soy sauce}を{取|と|to pass (to someone)}っていただけますか。
phrases.en: Could you pass me the soy sauce?
phrases.note: 〜ていただけますか is a notch politer than 〜てもらえますか: a safe choice with your host family in the first days.

phrases.jp: {おかわり||seconds, another helping}をお{願|ねが}いしてもいいですか。
phrases.note: おかわり = another helping (rice, soup, a drink). Asking for it is a compliment to the cook, not greedy.

phrases.jp: これは{何|なん}という{料理|りょうり|dish, cooking}ですか。
phrases.note: 〜という = called. Asking about the food is the easiest way to start a conversation at a Japanese table.

phrases.jp: ご{飯|はん}の{量|りょう|amount, portion}を{少なめ|すくなめ|on the small side}にしてもらえますか。
phrases.en: Could you make my rice portion a bit smaller?
phrases.note: 〜め softens an adjective: {少|すく}なめ = on the small side, {大|おお}きめ = on the big side. Also works at restaurants: ご{飯|はん}{少|すく}なめで.

phrases.jp: {遠慮|えんりょ|holding back, being shy}しないで、{どんどん||freely, as much as you like}{食|た}べて。
phrases.en: Don't hold back, eat as much as you like.
phrases.note: You'll hear this constantly from hosts. A graceful reply: じゃあ、お{言葉|ことば}に{甘|あま}えて (then I'll take you up on that).

dialogue_setting: At the low table in the Tanakas' living room, a clay pot bubbling in the middle.

dialogue.speaker: Keiko
dialogue.jp: {主人|しゅじん|(my) husband}に{頼|たの|to ask (a favour)}まれて、{今日|きょう}はりんご{鍋|なべ|hotpot}にしたのよ。
dialogue.en: My husband asked me to, so tonight it's apple nabe.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: りんごを{鍋|なべ|hotpot}に{入|い}れるんですか。{初|はじ}めて{見|み}ました！
dialogue.en: You put apples in nabe? I've never seen that!

dialogue.speaker: Tanaka-san
dialogue.jp: {鷹ノ原|たかのはら}のりんごは{甘|あま}い{ずら||(Nagano dialect) = でしょう, you'll see}。{遠慮|えんりょ|holding back, being shy}しないで{食べな|たべな|(casual) eat! = 食べなさい}。
dialogue.en: Takanohara apples are sweet, you'll see. Don't be shy, eat.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: すごくおいしいです。{おかわり||seconds, another helping}してもいいですか。
dialogue.en: It's really delicious. Can I have some more?

dialogue.speaker: Tanaka-san
dialogue.jp: {明日|あした}は{五時|ごじ}に{起|お}きるぞ。{遅|おく}れたら{妻|つま|(my) wife}に{怒|おこ|to get angry, tell off}られるからな。
dialogue.en: Tomorrow we get up at five. If you're late, my wife will tell you off.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: はい、{気|き}をつけます。{目覚まし|めざまし|alarm clock}を{二|ふた}つ{かけて||set (an alarm)}おきます！
dialogue.en: OK, I'll be careful. I'll set two alarms!

grammar.form: う-verbs: -a + れる ({頼|たの}む → {頼|たの}まれる, {怒|おこ}る → {怒|おこ}られる) · る-verbs: + られる ({見|み}る → {見|み}られる) · する → される · {来|く}る → {来|こ}られる
grammar.explanation: The person something happens to becomes the subject, and the one who does it gets に: {妻|つま}に{怒|おこ}られる = get told off by my wife. Japanese uses it far more than English, often for things that happen to you with a feeling of being bothered ({雨|あめ}に{降|ふ}られた = I got rained on). Careful: for る-verbs it looks the same as the potential form ({食|た}べられる = can eat or be eaten); context decides.

examples.jp: {電車|でんしゃ}で{足|あし}を{踏|ふ|to step on}まれました。
examples.en: Someone stepped on my foot on the train.

examples.jp: {子|こ}どもの{頃|ころ|time, when (子どもの頃 = as a child)}、よく{母|はは}に{褒|ほ|to praise}められた。
examples.en: As a kid I was often praised by my mum.

quiz.question: {先生|せんせい}に{名前|なまえ}を＿＿。
quiz.en: My name was called by the teacher.
quiz.explain: {呼|よ}ぶ → {呼|よ}ばれる: the teacher (に) did it to me. {呼|よ}ばせた is causative (made someone call), {呼|よ}べた is potential (could call).

kanji.where: From November it's everywhere: izakaya menus, supermarket shelves of {鍋|なべ}の{素|もと} (ready soup bases), {寄|よ}せ{鍋|なべ} and キムチ{鍋|なべ} at family restaurants.
kanji.related: {土鍋|どなべ} = the clay pot itself. {鍋|なべ}パーティー (鍋パ) = a hotpot party with friends.
kanji.breakdown: {鍋|なべ}: 金 metal on the left (pots were metal) + a part on the right that gives the sound か.

tip.title: Don't dive into the pot with your own chopsticks
tip.body: At a shared nabe there's usually an お{玉|たま|お玉 = ladle} (ladle) or {取|と}り{箸|ばし} (serving chopsticks): use those to fill your bowl, not the chopsticks you eat with. Often the host serves the first round for everyone, so wait a moment. Some people flip their chopsticks to serve, but many Japanese find that unhygienic, so asking for {取|と}り{箸|ばし} is the safer move.

challenge.prompt: Keiko offers you more rice, but you're full. Thank her, say it was delicious, and ask if you can help wash the dishes.
challenge.hint: お{腹|なか|お腹 = belly, stomach}いっぱい · お{皿|さら}を{洗|あら}う · 〜てもいいですか
challenge.model_answer: ありがとうございます。もうお{腹|なか|お腹 = belly, stomach}いっぱいです。とてもおいしかったです。お{皿|さら}を{洗|あら}ってもいいですか。
challenge.explanation: もうお{腹|なか}いっぱいです = I'm already full: the polite, natural way to say no to more. おいしかった is past because the meal is over. {洗|あら}ってもいいですか uses 〜てもいい to ask permission: 'May I wash the dishes?'

vocab.en: to take; to pass (something to someone)
on the small side, a little less

vocab.note: ご{遠慮|えんりょ}ください on signs = please refrain.
Older women's word for their husband; younger people say {夫|おっと} or {旦那|だんな}.

vocab.en: to get angry; to tell off

extras.title: Table phrases
extras.title_jp: {食卓|しょくたく|dining table}のひとこと
extras.intro: The set phrases you'll say or hear at every meal with your host family.

items.en: (before eating) Thank you for the food.
items.note: Said with hands together, to everyone, even at home.

items.en: (after eating) That was a feast, thank you.
items.note: Say it to the cook. At home the casual ごちそうさま is fine.

items.jp: お{腹|なか|お腹 = belly, stomach}いっぱいです。
{熱|あつ|hot (to the touch)}いから{気|き}をつけてね。
items.note: What you'll hear when the nabe is served.

extras.title: Asking nicely, step by step
extras.title_jp: お{願|ねが}いの{丁寧|ていねい|polite, courteous}さ
extras.intro: The same request from casual to very polite. With your hosts, start at the third and move down as you get closer.

items.jp: {取|と|to pass (to someone)}ってもらえますか。
{取|と|to pass (to someone)}っていただけますか。
items.en: Could you kindly pass it? (more polite)

items.jp: {取|と|to pass (to someone)}っていただけないでしょうか。
items.en: Would you mind passing it? (very polite, work and strangers)
